about: Number Quest catalog index - Phase 0 standards lock slice. Scope of THIS file: the Explorer intro (0.1) and Units 1-7 (22 steps) plus the Vault of Measures finale (7.4) - the complete Explorer street, 23 steps. Phase 0/1 covered Units 1-4; Phase 2 (2026-11-05) added Units 5-7 and the finale on the same terms, each step's LOCKED CCSS-M statement codes (primary / also / buildsToward, following the CS Quest units.json idiom), its Mathematical Practice spotlight, its stone and its teacher notes. Every ccss code cited here must appear in standards.json explorerCodes; buildsToward codes are preparation, never coverage, and the teacher page must label them so. Explorer Units 5-7, the Explorer finale, the whole Launchpad tier and the whole Pro tier are specced in math-course-spec.md sections 2.2/2.4/5 but are NOT built and NOT locked here - their statement locks land in their phases (see standards.json deferredClusters and placement.json deferred). Kids never see a standard code or a framework name; teachers see 'Number Quest - CCSS-M'.

program.name: Number Quest
program.standards: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSS-M, 2010), Explorer tier grades 3-5, locked Phase 0 for Units 1-4
program.tagline: Every number has a job to do.

teacherNotes: Number Quest is a standalone course: no CS Quest or Cyber Defenders knowledge is needed. The intro frames the Numberworks, Tally the cat, the Jumble and the Vault of Measures; it teaches no standard and its check, if any, is a routing preview, never assessed coverage.
units.title: Welcome to the Numberworks

explorer.primaryNote: A digit's value depends on where it sits. Grade 3 carries no freestanding place-value statement beyond rounding and operations (3.NBT.A), so this step's honest home is grade 4 NBT.A; grade 3 learners meet it through 4.NBT.A.2's read/write/compare work at three-digit depth in the mission scaling.
Rounding is choosing the nearest friendly number - to the nearest 10 or 100 in grade 3, to any place in grade 4. Decimal rounding (5.NBT.A.4) is the stretch shadow only.
CORRECTION to the spec's shorthand: grade 3 patterns are 3.OA.D.9, not OA.C. Grade 5's paired-pattern graphing (5.OA.B.3) is seeded here and taught in Unit 6 step 6.3.

teacherNotes: Open every worked example with an estimate (the course's 'Rough first' habit, MP1/MP2). Place value is taught as a pattern (each place ten times the next, MP7), not as column names to memorize.
units.title: The Counting House

explorer.primaryNote: CORRECTION to the spec's shorthand: grade 3 addition within 1000 is 3.NBT.A.2 (grade 3 has no NBT.B cluster); the standard algorithm is 4.NBT.B.4. Subtraction shares both statements and is the focus of step 2.2.

Subtraction taught both as taking away and as the gap between two numbers (counting up). Same two locked statements as 2.1, subtraction side; a step may share a statement with its sibling when the standard itself joins the operations.

The bar model is introduced here and reused in every later word-problem step. The computation statements sit in 'also': the step's new teaching is the two-step / multistep problem structure and the estimation check inside 4.OA.A.3.

teacherNotes: The bar model (Singapore CPA pictorial step) is taught once, here, before symbols: draw the story, see the missing piece, then write the equation. The unit's Jumble beat lives in 2.3: it added when the story said difference - learners find, name and fix it (MP3).
units.title: Joining & Splitting

explorer.primaryNote: Multiplication as equal groups and arrays. 3.MD.C (area) is buildsToward at CLUSTER level only - the array plants the seed; area itself is Unit 6 teaching under a later lock. 5.NBT.B.5 (standard algorithm fluency) is the stretch shadow.

Division as sharing and grouping. Honesty note: grade 3 states quotients without naming remainders; the remainder-as-a-decision teaching is locked to 4.NBT.B.6 and 4.OA.A.3 (interpreting remainders in multistep problems), shared with step 2.3.

This is where OA.C genuinely lives: fluency within 100 (3.OA.C.7), taught as strategies - properties (3.OA.B.5) and division as unknown-factor (3.OA.B.6) - never as bare memorization (spec section 8.3).

teacherNotes: Fluency missions are Dash gear: learners race their own ghost, never a classmate. Strategies are named in the deck (doubling, halving, near facts) so speed grows out of structure (MP7/MP8), per NCTM's build-fluency-from-understanding practice.
units.title: Groups & Shares

explorer.primaryNote: A fraction is a fair share of one whole AND a place on the number line - both halves of the grade 3 definition are locked and both must appear in the deck and in Fraction Factory's First Cuts.

Equivalence by re-cutting (the game's re-slice IS 4.NF.A.1's visual model), comparing by benchmark before machinery (4.NF.A.2). Every comparison in deck, check and game must keep the same-whole condition both standards require.

CORRECTION to the spec's shorthand: there is no grade 3 fraction-addition standard and no single 'NF.B' home - like-denominator addition is 4.NF.B.3, unlike-denominator addition (Fraction Factory's denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 genuinely reach it) is 5.NF.A.1 with word problems and benchmark estimation in 5.NF.A.2. 4.NF.B.4 is multiplication and is never cited here. The unit's flagship Jumble beat (1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6, adding the bottoms too) diagnoses exactly the 5.NF.A.1 misconception.

teacherNotes: Cut real paper cakes before the deck: equivalence lands in hands first (CPA). Fraction Factory is this unit's home game and Tally the cat's debut - her sprite is extracted from Fraction Factory, never redrawn (house rule).
units.title: The Bakery

explorer.primaryNote: Measuring is counting units: length, mass and volume are all counted the same way, and every metric conversion in this step is the same measure wearing a new name (x10, x100, x1000). The measuring statements are grade 3 (3.MD.A.2) with relative unit sizes from grade 4 (4.MD.A.1); multi-step conversion problems are 5.MD.A.1 and are built toward, not claimed.

Elapsed time is taught as distance on a number line: hop the hours, then the minutes left over. Telling time and measuring intervals is 3.MD.A.1; the timetable word problems also work 4.MD.A.2 (operations on intervals of time with diagrams), cited as also-covers because the step's problems are one-interval, not the full range of that statement.

CORRECTION to the spec's shorthand: there is no grade 3-5 money statement of its own in CCSS-M. Money word problems live in 4.MD.A.2, which is this step's primary; the 'money is decimals in disguise' link (a dollar as 100 cents, $2.35 read as a decimal) is grade 4 cluster 4.NF.C and is cited as a builds-toward CLUSTER only, never as coverage. Change is taught as the gap on the bar, the Unit 2 subtraction model with money names.

teacherNotes: Bring real tools before the deck: a meter stick, a kitchen scale, a measuring jug, a handful of coins. Measuring is counting units, and it lands in the hands first (CPA). The unit's Jumble beat is in 5.3, where it reads $2.05 as two dollars and five cents and forgets the zero that holds the place.
units.title: The Measure Shop

explorer.primaryNote: Shapes are sorted by properties a child can test: count the sides, find the square corners, check for parallel sides. Categories and shared attributes are 3.G.A.1; classifying by parallel lines and angle size is 4.G.A.2; identifying the parts (4.G.A.1) rides along as also-covers. The full property hierarchy is 5.G.B.4, built toward here and taught in 6.3. No game ships for this step yet (Builder's Yard is a later phase): the mission is a classroom shape hunt, and the step completes on its check, exactly as the intro does.

CORRECTION to the spec's shorthand ('MD.C for area AND perimeter'): area is MD.C, but perimeter at grade 3 is 3.MD.D.8 and the rectangle formulas are 4.MD.A.3. The step teaches both moves side by side on purpose: perimeter is the fence (add the sides), area is the carpet (multiply the sides), and the famous confusion between them is the lesson, not a slip. Area as an attribute and counting unit squares (3.MD.C.5, 3.MD.C.6) are also covered on the way.

Lines (parallel, perpendicular, rays) and symmetry as a fold are grade 4 (4.G.A.1, 4.G.A.3). Grid addresses are the grade 5 coordinate plane's front door (5.G.A.1), with points read in context (5.G.A.2). This is also where step 1.3's builds-toward lands: graphing the pairs a pattern generates is 5.OA.B.3, taught here. Sorting shapes into a family tree by their properties (5.G.B.3) is covered; the full hierarchy statement (5.G.B.4) remains builds-toward. The unit's Jumble beat is here: it swaps the two numbers of a grid address.

teacherNotes: String and pegs (or chalk on the playground) before the deck: build one fence and one carpet with the same string and let the class feel the difference between around and inside. The unit's Jumble beat is in 6.3, where it reads a grid address backwards and lands one square off.
units.title: The Building Yard

explorer.primaryNote: A scaled bar graph is a picture that answers: read how many, then how many more (3.MD.B.3). Line plots of fractional measurements join in the same step (4.MD.B.4); solving problems by re-sharing the amounts on a line plot is 5.MD.B.2, built toward and finished in 7.2. The mission plays Data Detective's Chart It chapter, borrowed from CS Quest with its own cases untouched.

The data starts with the question: two choices or a handful, never a list of twenty. Generating measurement data and plotting it is 3.MD.B.4; the class survey's own chart re-uses 7.1's scaled graphs (3.MD.B.3, also-covers), and sharing a total equally from a line plot reaches 5.MD.B.2 in simple cases (also-covers). The mission plays Data Detective's My Data chapter: the learner's own survey, tallied, charted and claimed.

ENRICHMENT, flagged honestly: chance language (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) has NO CCSS code before grade 6 statistics and probability, so this step cites nothing anywhere - not in the lock, not here, not on the teacher map. It teaches judgement with words and a tally of real spins, nothing more, and nothing in grade 3-5 coverage depends on it. The mission plays Would You Rather's Numbers topic, a bank of sure-thing-versus-chance dilemmas built for this step.

The finale's graded spine is measures, as its name promises: telling time and intervals (3.MD.A.1), measurement word problems (4.MD.A.2) and conversions used in multi-step problems (5.MD.A.1). The other six locks are reviewed, not re-taught: one representative code per workshop is cited as also-covers (place value 4.NBT.A.3, groups 3.OA.A.3, fractions 3.NF.A.3, shapes 4.G.A.2, charts 3.MD.B.3), and the mission's Vault Run circuit plays one question per lock. The Vault game itself is a later phase; the finale ships as this sequenced mixed mission, the Cyber Defenders fallback pattern.

teacherNotes: Collect real answers before the deck: one class question with a handful of choices, tallied on the board. A chart of the class's own answers is the one chart nobody has to be persuaded to read. Step 7.3 is enrichment and says so on the map: chance words are judgement practice, not coverage. The unit's Jumble beat is in 7.3, where it calls a one-in-six chance 'impossible' - and the Vault finale (7.4) is where the Jumble's whole story ends.
units.title: The Fairground
